video.title: Why Your Wrist Hurts, and How to Fix It

classification.reason: The coach provides actionable cues instructing players to make contact during the early stretch-release phase rather than driving with the late follow-through.

problem.title_as_question: Why does your wrist hurt on the forehand, and how can you fix it?
problem.definition: Players experience wrist fatigue and pain when attempting to generate spin and power by actively driving and flexing the wrist through the late follow-through rather than relying on early elastic release.
problem.target_player: players experiencing wrist pain or trying to generate heavy topspin

symptoms.description: The wrist and hand fatigue repeatedly and eventually develop pain.
The ball lacks forward drive and penetration when struck with the late rolling portion of the swing.
The wrist visibly enters active flexion past the hitting slot to push the racket through.

causes.statement: Contacting the ball too late forces the player to actively push and flex the wrist through the ball to generate forward drive.
Small muscles in the wrist and hand are not strong enough to actively drive the heavy racket forward and are only built for passive elastic support.
Forward back-to-front racket head speed dissipates immediately after contact release, leaving only rolling rotational speed.
The player's brain misinterprets the fast rolling speed during the follow-through as the primary hitting acceleration zone.

angles.summary: Uses Federer's forehand sequence to demonstrate that maximum back-to-front acceleration occurs right at contact rather than in the follow-through.
Explains that high racket speed after contact consists of pronation and internal rotation rather than forward driving speed.
Explains that ninety percent of the windshield wiper movement happens after contact, so players should not anchor their hitting action on it.
Explains that players mistakenly perceive the high speed of the follow-through roll as their hitting action because of the sensation of speed.
Points out that small wrist muscles are intended to transfer elastic energy from big muscles rather than actively flex to push racket weight.

solutions.summary: Remind yourself to find the hitting slot earlier in the stretch-release elastic throwing sensation rather than delaying contact.
Focus on striking the ball with only the first five percent of the windshield wiper motion and let the rest occur passively as follow-through.
Hit the ball during the early stretch-release phase and refrain from actively driving or forcing the wrist through during the later roll.
